docs.title: Getting started with a private model (v2ecoli)
docs.text:
compose-api runs simulations for you on UConn Health's computing cluster: you send it a model, it runs it there, and you download the results. Some models on it are private. v2ecoli, Eran Agmon's lab's whole-cell model of E. coli, is one of them: only people who have been given access can see it or run it.

You run v2ecoli from the workbench, a web page that runs on your own computer. It shows v2ecoli's models and sends the runs to compose-api for you. This page takes you from nothing to a finished run.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The Google account whose email you gave us. Access is tied to that email address, so sign in with that account every time.
  • A GitHub account that has been given access to v2ecoli's code (it is private too).
  • macOS or Linux. On Windows, use a lab Mac or Linux machine.
  • A terminal: Terminal on macOS, any terminal on Linux. You type every command below there.

docs.title: 1. Check your access on the web
docs.text:
1. Open https://compose.cam.uchc.edu/ui.
  2. Click Sign in (top right) and choose Google. Use the Google account whose email you gave us. The first time, this also creates your compose-api account.
  3. Open the account menu (top right, where Sign in was). It shows the email you're signed in with and, under it, your roles. repo-v2ecoli should be one of them, for example:

text Roles: repo-v2ecoli, user

repo-v2ecoli is your access to v2ecoli; user is what every account has.

Don't see repo-v2ecoli?

  • Check the email in the menu. If it isn't the one you gave us, choose Sign out and sign in again with the right Google account.
  • If you signed in to compose-api before your access was set up, sign out and back in: your roles are read when you sign in.
  • Still missing? Ask Alex Patrie on Slack, and tell Alex the email the menu shows. (Slack, not a GitHub issue: anyone can read an issue.)

docs.title: uv
docs.text:
uv installs Python tools, and fetches a suitable version of Python for you:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Close the terminal and open a new one.

docs.title: A C compiler
docs.text:
v2ecoli compiles parts of itself when it installs. On macOS, run:

xcode-select --install

If it says the tools are already installed, you're set. On Linux (Ubuntu), run sudo apt install build-essential.

docs.title: v2ecoli and the workbench
docs.text:
v2ecoli's code is on GitHub. Install the GitHub CLI from https://cli.github.com, then sign in to GitHub once:

gh auth login

Choose GitHub.com, then HTTPS, and sign in with your GitHub account in the browser. Then download v2ecoli and install it with the workbench:

gh repo clone vivarium-collective/v2ecoli
cd v2ecoli
uv sync --extra report

The last line installs v2ecoli, the workbench and everything they need. The first time, it takes several minutes.

docs.title: 3. Start the workbench
docs.text:
In the v2ecoli folder:

uv run vivarium-workbench serve --backend-base-url https://compose.cam.uchc.edu

It prints a few lines, ending with Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:<port>. Open that address in your browser. Leave the terminal open: closing it stops the workbench. To stop it yourself, press Ctrl+C there.

Next time, open a terminal, cd v2ecoli, and run the same uv run vivarium-workbench serve ... line.

docs.title: 4. Sign in to compose-api (once)
docs.text:
The workbench sends your runs to compose-api as you, so you sign in once.

  1. In the left column, click Process, then click a model in the Registry panel (for example ecoli_single_cell).
  2. Beside its Runs: Cloud label, click Sign in.
  3. Your browser opens Google's sign-in. Choose the same Google account as in step 1, then come back to the workbench. A panel in the bottom-right corner says what is happening (click it to close it).
  4. When you're signed in, Sign in disappears from beside Runs: Cloud.

If the workbench runs on another computer than the browser you're using (over SSH, say), sign in with a code instead: add #github to the workbench's address (for example http://127.0.0.1:8001/#github, with your own port), and under Account, in the compose-api row, click Use a code instead. The panel in the corner then shows a link and a code to enter on any device.

You stay signed in: the sign-in is kept in your computer's password store (Keychain on macOS), so you won't need to do this again for a while. If Sign in appears beside Runs: Cloud again later, click it again.

On Linux, the sign-in is kept in the desktop's password service (GNOME Keyring or KWallet). If signing in stops with a message about the credential store or keyring, use a desktop session where one runs, or ask Alex.

docs.title: 5. Run the single cell
docs.text:
1. In the left column, click Process.
  2. In the Registry panel, type single in the search box, then click ecoli_single_cell: one cell growing. Its card says Runs: Cloud: the workbench sends its runs to compose-api.
  3. Below the picture of the model, set Duration to 60 (seconds of the cell's life), then click ▶ Run.
  4. After a minute or two it shows ✓ complete. Under Outputs, Results lists what the run recorded (61 rows, one per simulated second), and ⬇ Download results saves them.

Your runs are private: only you can see them.

For now, compose-api runs two v2ecoli models: ecoli_single_cell, and ecoli_lineage for many generations (step 6). The others also say Runs: Cloud, but pressing ▶ Run on them shows Run failed — no results produced. That's expected until compose-api can run them, which is coming.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Up to 1,000 s works for everyone. Longer runs need the long-runs role. As it is set up, everyone on the v2ecoli list gets that role when they first sign in, as they get repo-v2ecoli. If a run past 1,000 s fails with compose-api's message "compose-api refused the run: Invalid interval time, it has to be between 0 and 1000; up to 86400 with the long-runs role", check that you signed in with the email you gave us (step 1), then tell Alex.
  • With ecoli_single_cell, keep runs to 2,400 s or less: the cell divides at about 2,500 s, and a single cell has nowhere to put its daughters, so the run ends with no results. To go past a division, use ecoli_lineage (step 6).

If a run fails or is refused, note the message the workbench shows and tell Alex (see Help).

docs.title: 6. Many generations: ecoli_lineage
docs.text:
ecoli_lineage follows one cell through its generations: at each division one daughter carries on, so a run of many generations costs one cell at a time, not a colony that doubles each generation.

  1. In the left column, click Process. In the Registry panel, type lineage in the search box, then click ecoli_lineage.
  2. Set Duration to the seconds of cell life you want, then click ▶ Run. A generation is about 2,500 to 2,900 s of cell life: for three generations (two divisions), set about 7700. Runs past 1,000 s need the long-runs role (see Limits above).
  3. Wait for ✓ complete, then ⬇ Download results.

What we measured on one run (seed 0, 25 Nov), as a guide rather than a promise: divisions at 2,527 s and 5,431 s, about 6 s of cell life per second of waiting, so 7,700 s took about 23 minutes. The longest run compose-api takes is 86,400 s of cell life, roughly 30 generations and about 4 hours.

What the results hold: one row per simulated second. Each row lists the cells alive then (one, in a lineage) by their id, with:

  • id: the generation is the number of _ in it minus one: a_0 is the first cell, a_0_0 its daughter, a_0_0_0 the next. The time a new id first appears is that division's time.
  • mass: the cell's dry mass, in femtograms. A daughter starts at half her mother's last value.
  • length: the cell's length, in micrometres.
  • volume: the volume gained since that cell's birth, not its total volume.

Several seeds: run once per seed. Before ▶ Run, set the card's seed field to a different number for each run, and download each run's results.

If a run is cancelled or stops before the end, nothing from it is kept yet: run it again.

If the workbench marks a long run failed with a message ending "(the run was sent: it is compose-NNNNN on compose-api, which may finish it all the same)", the workbench lost touch with the run, but compose-api may still finish it. The workbench can't load that run's results afterwards: they stay on compose-api under that run number. Tell Alex the number: Alex can get them for you.

docs.title: Help
docs.text: • Questions, or something didn't work: ask Alex Patrie on Slack, or open an issue at https://github.com/biosimulations/compose-api/issues (anyone can read it, so leave out your email and anything private).

docs.title: Adding a simulator to the registry
docs.text:
In registry_env and in every composed environment (mash-ups included), compose-api runs a process class only if its module belongs to an entry at level tested or higher, as set in compose_api/registry/manifest.yaml or as computed from the compliance cases of the composed version (registry/validation.py). A prebuilt image's classes are not looked up: an administrator vouches for the image by registering it as a version (api/routers/simulation.py). This page is for anyone who wants a wrapper repository (a viva-* workspace, or any process-bigraph package) to run here, and for the person who reviews that change. The checklist is the pull request template registry-entry.md; this page says what it asks for and why.

GitHub fills a pull request from a template in a PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/ directory only when the compare URL names it: https://github.com/biosimulations/compose-api/compare/main...<branch>?quick_pull=1&template=registry-entry.md (GitHub: query parameters). Opened any other way, paste the template's text into the description.

docs.title: Three paths
docs.text:
1. Listed through viva-catalog. This never runs. registry/catalog.py reads viva-catalog's modules.json and writes registry/catalog.yaml: every wrapper at level listed, pinned to the commit its branch pointed at that day. The file is generated and never edited by hand. The service runs tested or higher, so admission refuses a listed entry's classes. Listing makes a repository discoverable and grants nothing.
  2. A manifest entry, by pull request, at the level the evidence supports. The entry names the package, how it installs, the modules it provides and the evidence for its level. Entries change only by pull request, and an entry in manifest.yaml takes precedence over the catalog.yaml entry with the same id. Administrators register environment versions through the API, never entries.
  3. After the merge, below: a release, then a signed-in run builds the environment.

docs.title: After the merge
docs.text:
• The manifest is a versioned file in the package, read at call time, so an entry takes effect with the next compose-api release.
  • An entry with empty bundles is in no declared environment. When nothing covers the entries a document names, the first run by a signed-in caller makes a mash-up of exactly those entries, with what they requires: a pixi.toml generated from the entries, locked in an unprivileged Job, built on the privileged builder, read back, and checked by each member entry's compliance cases (docs/plan-environment-composition.md, D7.4, D7.5). Later runs with the same set reuse that version.
  • An anonymous caller whose run needs a mash-up that does not exist gets a 401 and causes no build. At most two are locked or built at once, and a set of packages that conflict is a 409 with pixi's explanation (environments/lifecycle.py). If the first lock or build of a set fails, later runs of that set get a 409 until an administrator makes a new version.
  • The cases decide the entry's level in that version: tested when they pass, failed when one does not, untested without cases. An entry whose cases are still running is refused there until they finish; one with no cases, or whose cases cannot run (a missing file is a logged warning), keeps the manifest's level for admission (composition plan, 5b, 5c; environments/compliance_runs.py). A module of the entry that does not import in the version's image refuses every class under it there (module-imports).
  • Moving the pin is another manifest pull request and release; a pin that moves never starts a build by itself (D7.7).
  • Every composed version installs the core that environments.yaml names under composition.core when the version is made: process-bigraph 1.11.1 and bigraph-schema 1.8.3 (1.9.1 and 1.8.1 before). A version keeps the pixi.toml and the lock it was made with, and its image installs that lock unchanged (environments/service.py, environments/pixi.py), so a new core reaches only versions made after the release that carries it. Existing versions, mash-ups included, keep theirs, and later runs of the same set still use them. process-bigraph 1.11.1 no longer requires scipy, sympy or matplotlib, as 1.9.1 did, so an entry that imports one must declare it.
  • vivarium-tyssue's mash-up keeps its version on 1.9.1, which runs as before. On the current core its sheet-relaxation case fails while the composite is built: bigraph-schema 1.8.3 cannot merge a table (a Frame) with no update, which bigraph-schema 1.8.4 fixes (bigraph-schema #209), and process-bigraph 1.11.1 requires bigraph-schema below 1.8.4. A version made on this core that includes vivarium-tyssue therefore records it failed and refuses its classes. That version stays so: once process-bigraph allows 1.8.4 and the core moves to it, an administrator makes a new version of that environment, since a run makes only a mash-up's first version (D7.7).
  • A package that publishes its own image is registered by an administrator as a version of a named environment (D8.3), which needs its own line in environments.yaml.

docs.title: Writing the entry
docs.text:
Preferred: generate it with vivarium-workbench compose-entry, which produces the entry and checks it (see its --help), and paste both into the pull request. A hand-written entry is accepted: copy the closest one in manifest.yaml and say in the pull request that it is hand-written, and why. By shape: viva-basic-processes (git, nothing else), pbsim-common (git with requires and types), viva-pde-particle (git with conda: engines, extras, and its own image), pb-multiscale-actin (a PyPI release), smoldyn-vcell (a wheel by URL and sha256).

A component often needs library entries beside it (kind: library: an engine, or a pin on a floating dependency; install or conda, no module_roots). They install code like any other entry and are reviewed the same way. Their level gates nothing: what runs is a component's classes (environments/lifecycle.py, composable).

An entry that provides the same simulator as an existing one (often the same class names) says so with alternative_to: <standard entry id>. The standard entry is what the service's own runs use (SED-ML solvers, suites); the alternative keeps its own level and runs where admitted, and the catalog shows it as an alternative. viva-copasi and viva-tellurium are alternatives to pbsim-common until the two families are reconciled. The standard entry must be a component that is not itself an alternative (tests/registry/test_manifest.py).

docs.title: Check that it locks
docs.text:
A signed-in first run of an entry makes a mash-up of exactly that entry and what it requires: pixi_toml() writes a pixi workspace, an unprivileged Job locks it with pixi exec --spec git -- pixi lock in the image environments.yaml names, and a lock that does not resolve is recorded as a failed version. Later runs of that entry set then get a 409 until an administrator makes a new version (environments/service.py, environments/lifecycle.py), so an entry that cannot lock must not reach a release at tested, and no check above locks one. To run the same step before asking, in a clone of compose-api whose manifest.yaml has the entry (an entry that is only in catalog.yaml has no install, so there is nothing to lock):

ENTRY=viva-ketchup      # the entry's id
W=$(mktemp -d)
uv run python - "$ENTRY" > "$W/pixi.toml" <<'PY'
import datetime
import sys

from compose_api.environments.pixi import DEFAULT_PYTHON_VERSION, ComposedSpec, pixi_toml
from compose_api.registry.environments import load_environments
from compose_api.registry.manifest import load_manifest

composition = load_environments().composition
entry = next(e for e in load_manifest().entries if e.id == sys.argv[1])
now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC).replace(microsecond=0)
spec = ComposedSpec("lock-check", (entry,), tuple(sorted(composition.core.items())), composition.platform, DEFAULT_PYTHON_VERSION, now)
print(pixi_toml(spec), end="")
PY
IMAGE=$(uv run python -c 'from compose_api.registry.environments import load_environments; print(load_environments().composition.pixi_image)')
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -v "$W":/work -w /work "$IMAGE" pixi exec --spec git -- pixi lock
grep '^- pypi: git+' "$W/pixi.lock" | grep -v '?rev='     # git sources pinned to no commit; empty is what is wanted

--platform linux/amd64 is the Job's platform (on Apple silicon the arm64 image fails whenever a source build is needed); HOME=/tmp keeps pixi's cache inside the container (on macOS a cache on the mounted folder fails with "failed to link ... Invalid argument"). What a lock does not show: the privileged build, the run, this entry together with others, or a later day (exclude-newer is now, and a git branch tip moves).

docs.title: What CI checks
docs.text:
These run on every pull request, so a change that breaks one is red before a reviewer reads it:

  • An entry is pinned by version or commit, has module_roots if it is a component, and ids are unique (registry/manifest.py).
  • An install names exactly one of pypi with its exact version, git with a full 40-character commit (never a branch), or url (an https .whl) with its sha256. requires names entries that exist.
  • Every entry above listed has evidence, and every library says how it installs (tests/registry/test_manifest.py).
  • Each declared environment still composes: no two entries install one distribution, no conda package is asked for with two specs, requires are listed, bundles and entries agree (registry/environments.py, tests/registry/test_environments.py).
  • Compliance cases are checked only for the entries a test names, today pbsim-common, viva-basic-processes and viva-pde-particle (tests/environments/test_compliance.py). No test walks every entry's cases, so a new entry's case is checked only by a test its pull request adds or by the reviewer, with the command in the template.
  • Whether an entry's environment locks is checked by none of these (see "Check that it locks").

Locally: uv run python -m pytest tests/registry tests/environments/test_compliance.py -q (the database-backed tests need Docker), and make check for the lint and type checks (CLAUDE.md).

docs.title: What only a reviewer can check, and why
docs.text:
• Provenance. An entry is pinned to a release or a commit (composition plan, "What is a safe component"). The reviewer approves that commit, not the repository, so the template asks who controls the repository, that the hash is on its default branch or a tag, and, for a new pin, which files changed since the old one. A commit on the default branch or a tag is also the test plan-entry-updates.md proposes for moved commits.
  • One hash, one repository. Only install.commit is validated, and it is what pixi installs (environments/pixi.py). commit: and the source URL are what people read, and nothing ties them to install: not the hash, nor the repository.
  • Install-time code. The build runs package code as root on the privileged builder, and locking reads package metadata, which can run build code, in an unprivileged Job (simulation/build_k8s.py). The reviewer reads the build backend, its requirements and any setup.py, hook or build script. A pypi pin is built too when the release has no wheel for the environment's Python, and for a url pin the reviewer asks how the wheel was built (the smoldyn-vcell entry names the workflow that built it).
  • Import-time code. process-bigraph builds its core with bigraph-schema's allocate_core, which imports the modules of every installed distribution that requires bigraph-schema (bigraph-schema 1.8.3, package/discover.py: is_process_library, load_local_modules). bigraph-schema caches that walk's index under ~/.cache/bigraph-schema, but a run starts the image with --compat, whose home is empty each time, so every run walks again. Import-time code in anything a wheel ships, and in every dependency that requires bigraph-schema, can therefore run whether or not a document names it. That is why the template asks about packages outside module_roots.
  • Distribution name. The generated pixi.toml keys the dependency by the name install derives (the repository's name for git), and two entries with one name are a composition problem. [project].name at the commit should be that name.
  • Dependencies. A composed environment installs the package's declared dependencies, so a development tool among them lands in every run image, and a git or URL reference is not covered by the pin. The pin freezes the package, not what it depends on: those resolve when the version is locked, no newer than the lock's exclude-newer date (environments/pixi.py). The composition also fixes Python and the core's process-bigraph and bigraph-schema versions (environments.yaml), so a package whose bounds exclude them cannot be locked with the others. viva-pde-particle keeps vivarium-workbench behind a workbench extra for this reason (its pyproject.toml). A git package's own [tool.uv.sources] are followed as well: a source that sends a dependency to a branch pins nothing, and the lock takes that branch's tip, and the tip's own sources, the day it runs ("Check that it locks" lists them).
  • Config-driven imports. The address check is the only gate (registry/validation.py) and sees only address values. A class that imports or runs what its config names escapes it: EnsembleRunner imported a module:function from its config, and viva-pde-particle#67 replaced it (composition plan, 7c-4). The types items are imported by the runner before every run (environments/runner.py), so each should be in the entry's own package. Code the config or a submitted file supplies is the same hole: vivarium-tyssue's SBMLCellCycle evaluates expressions from its config, so its module is not a root.
  • Submitted files a class deserializes. A file in the upload that a class unpickles runs code too. pandas unpickles HDF5 object columns and some attributes, and submission refuses an HDF5 file that holds them (registry/uploads.py). No other format is checked, so a class that loads a submitted pickle, joblib file or numpy array with allow_pickle must not reach tested.
  • Module roots. Admission gives a module to the entry with the longest matching root and refuses a module no root contains (Manifest.entry_for_module). A root that is not what the package ships makes its own classes unrunnable, a generic root such as app claims every module beneath it, and a root nested inside another entry's takes classes from it; nothing compares one entry's roots with another's (Manifest validates ids and requires). catalog.yaml's roots come from viva-catalog's package field, which registry/catalog.py copies without checking. Many of them do not match what the repository ships: a workspace whose package is pbg_<x> is recorded as viva_<x>, viva_Mgen is listed for a package that ships viva_mgen, and some omit a package the workspace also ships (a compatibility shim or a studies package). Take the roots from what the build backend ships (hatch or setuptools packages or packages.find, maturin module-name), not from the repository's name. A directory that exists in the tree is not proof that the wheel ships it: read the packaging settings.
  • Non-Python needs. What PyPI cannot supply (a Node.js bridge, MPI, a C++ engine) belongs under conda:. Two entries that list one conda package with different specs cannot share an environment: a mash-up of them is refused with a 409 at run time, and CI checks only the declared environments (registry/environments.py).
  • Step outputs. step-outputs-replace refuses a Step whose output ports add or append (float, integer, array, list, set and the like, also inside map[...]; environments/compliance.py). It runs when a built version is read back, so a Step that fails it is found only after the merge and costs a second pull request (viva-pde-particle#69, then a new pin). Reading its outputs() first avoids that.
  • Evidence and the case. evidence says what supports the level, and which commit it is about. The case's description should say where its expected values come from: a hand calculation (viva-basic-processes), a reference report (pbsim-common), or the package's own earlier output run through compose-api's runner (viva-pde-particle). load_cases returns an empty list for a directory it does not find, which looks the same as "no case", so the template's command prints each case with its problems.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text: The service runs a component whose level is tested or higher, as the manifest sets it or as a composed version computed it from the entry's cases (HPC_MINIMUM_LEVEL, registry/validation.py); listed and installable components do not run. Raising a level needs its evidence in evidence (the header of manifest.yaml). validated and curated need more, set out in docs/strategy.md, decision 5. Ask for the level the evidence supports and say which evidence it is; the reviewer decides.

docs.title: Accepted findings
docs.text:
When a version's image is read back, generic checks run over its classes (environments/compliance.py), and a class that fails one is refused in that version. One check, step-outputs-replace, fails a Step whose outputs add or append, because a Step may fire more than once in a tick and would count its results twice. Some Steps add deliberately and cannot fire twice, for example one gated by update_condition to once per scheduled solve. An entry can accept such a failure for one of its own classes:

accepted_findings:
  - component: v2ecoli.processes.metabolism.Metabolism
    check: step-outputs-replace
    reason: gated by update_condition to once per scheduled solve; its exchange deltas count once
    evidence: tests/test_metabolism_gate.py

The finding stays on the version's record, marked with the reason, and the class is admitted. reason and evidence are both required; only an entry installed from git can accept a finding, only for its own classes (not a nested root's), and only step-outputs-replace (a class that does not import is never admitted). A composed version records the acceptances it was made with, and only those apply in it: a prebuilt or shared version accepts nothing. An acceptance therefore takes effect with a new version, which needs the entry's next commit (usually the one that adds the evidence test): a version of the same commit resolves to the same lock as the one before, and is not made (unless compose-api's runner has changed since, which makes a new version). evidence is a test in the entry's own repository, showing why the check's concern does not apply. A reviewer reads it as they would any evidence for a level. When a version is made, its lock Job checks first that each evidence path is a file at the entry's pinned commit (a private repository's through its token), and one that is not fails the version, saying which.

docs.title: A private repository
docs.text:
An entry whose repository is private names the Auth0 role of the people who may use it, access_role: <role> (registry/access.py; docs/plan-private-repo-usage.md). Its metadata is in this public repository like any entry's, but the service hides it, its environments and their runs from everyone without the role, and refuses its classes to them as unregistered ones. CI refuses such an entry in the shared environment, a solver, a public entry's requires, a module root another entry shares, or with compliance-case files other than its document (tests/registry/test_access.py). The role itself is created and assigned in the BioSim Auth0 tenant.

The service fetches the repository through its own GitHub App, compose-api-private-source, which reads repository contents and nothing else. The App is private to vivarium-collective, where an owner of the organization installs it on the repository. A repository in another organization needs the App made public, or an App of its own. The entry installs from git at a commit (install: {git, commit}). Each Job that locks or builds one of its versions gets a token for that version's private repositories alone, valid for an hour, in a Secret the Job owns. The build is made from a clone taken before it starts, so the token is in neither the image nor anything the service records. An environment's private repositories come from one organization. When no token can be had (the App is not installed, or GitHub is down), the request is a 503 and no version is recorded, so it can simply be made again (compose_api/environments/source_credentials.py).

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: A proof-of-concept browser UI for this API lives in webapp/. It is a static single-page app built with Nuxt 4, Nuxt UI 4 and Tailwind v4, the same stack as the BioSimulations platform frontend (biosimulations/platform, frontend/), whose shell, theme and page patterns it adapts. The API serves it at /ui on the same host, and / redirects there.

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text:
Page API operations /ui/ dashboard: counts by status, recent runs list-simulations, /version /ui/simulations: paged and filterable by status, simulator, date, labels (key:value) and tags; label and tag chips filter the list; where each run ran ("Ran in"), and the runs of one environment, version or simulator (linked from their pages); download results.zip list-simulations, get-simulation-results-file /ui/simulations/new: upload a .pbg, .omex or .sbml, or a curated COPASI/Tellurium time course from SBML. Registry rejections are listed address by address run-simulation, run-copasi, run-tellurium /ui/simulations/{id}: where it ran (its environment version, or its simulator for a run from before versions), status (polled until terminal), SLURM and container-build details, live event log, span tree and Chrome trace (for Perfetto), datasets with inline previews (images, CSV/TSV plotted with Plotly, JSON, text) get-simulation, get-simulation-status, get-simulator-build-status, get-simulation-events, get-simulation-trace, get-simulation-trace-chrome, list-datasets, get-dataset-content, get-simulation-results-file /ui/datasets: every run's files list-datasets, get-dataset-content /ui/datasets/{id}: one dataset full width in its viewers (a results bundle file by file) get-dataset, get-dataset-content, get-dataset-file /ui/composites/new: write a composite in .pblang, checked as you type, and run it (below) list-environments, get-environment-manifest, run-simulation /ui/sedml: a SED-ML archive (upload, BioModels, biosimulations.org) previewed and run on several solvers (plan-sedml.md) preview-sedml, run-sedml, search-biomodels, get-biomodel-omex, run-biomodel, search-biosimulations-projects, get-biosimulations-omex, run-biosimulations-project, list-solvers /ui/comparisons, /ui/comparisons/{id}: a task's runs, scores per report and data set, overlays of data sets and SED-ML plots list-comparisons, get-comparison, get-comparison-series, list-datasets, get-dataset-content /ui/suites, /ui/suites/{name}: regression and reproducibility suites, their runs (each with the environment versions it ran in), agreement, references and drift from the baseline per model; "Run the suite" (signed in) picks a version of each environment its solvers use and confirms first; with suites:curate, mark, edit and clear each solver's known problems, each confirmed (plan-known-problems) list-suites, list-suite-runs, get-suite-run, run-suite, list-solvers, list-environment-versions, list-suite-problems, mark-suite-problem, edit-suite-problem, clear-suite-problem /ui/environments: where composites run, and the simulators runs used before environments had versions; /ui/environments/{name}: its image, versions (each linked to its runs), registry entries, and every class it provides with its config and ports (#Name opens on one); administration, below list-environments, get-environment-manifest, list-environment-versions, list-simulators /ui/environments/{name}/versions/{n}: one version: its installed packages and a diff against another version, its lock and the pixi/uv files that recreate it, its entries with their compliance cases, its classes, and its runs get-environment-version, export-environment-version, get-environment-version-compliance /ui/simulators/{id}: one simulator (a container definition, identified by its hash): its definition, the versions it is, and its runs. A simulator from before versions belongs to no environment, and this page is the only place it is described get-simulator /ui/catalog: every registry entry with its curation level, pin and evidence, and the environments that run its classes (plan-sedml.md, "Concepts") list-registry-entries

Viewers are registered per dataset type (webapp/app/viewers/registry.ts, plan). Each one declares which datasets it fits (by kind, media type and attributes) and is an async component, so a viewer and its libraries download only when first opened. /ui/datasets/<id> opens a dataset full width; the table's preview shows the same viewers. Built in: composite (below), image, table (plotted when numeric), text, a Plotly figure (application/vnd.plotly.v1+json, SED-ML plots), and for results bundles (*.fenics) a statistics view and a 3D view (vtk.js) read chunk by chunk with zarrita from /datasets/{id}/files/. The 3D view draws the bundle's web extension (a precomputed surface per domain, viva-pde-particle docs/web-bundle.md) coloured by one variable, fetches one row per frame, shows particles, and follows a running simulation.

The submitted composite (the input dataset: a .pbg document, or an OMEX archive holding one or more, found as the service finds them at submission: .pbg and .json members, nested .omex archives at most three deep; with several, a picker chooses one) opens in the composite viewer (webapp/app/viewers/CompositeViewer.vue): the document is decompiled in the browser into .pblang text by process-bigraph-lang (the npm package of its dsl/), checked, and shown read-only in Monaco with the checker's findings as markers and as a list. The Document tab shows the process-bigraph JSON that was submitted and run, re-indented only (every token as submitted: 100.0 stays a float), with a download; the Graph tab draws the wiring (viewers/composite/layout.ts, stores left, processes and steps right, a link per wired port, nested composites below). The checker resolves addresses against interface manifests: one per environment documents run in, generated in CI inside each image and served by the API at GET /registry/environments and GET /registry/environments/{name}/manifest (same origin; in development, from whatever NUXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE points at). The viewer uses the manifest of the environment the run used (a prebuilt run is matched by its image's repository, whatever its digest). Hovering a class's name in the text, or its address in the document, shows the class's interface from that manifest (viewers/composite/interfaces.ts), linked to its environment's page; the "checked against" badge links there too.

Writing a composite (/ui/composites/new, or "Edit a copy" from the viewer) opens .pblang text in an editable Monaco with process-bigraph-lang's language server running in a web worker (viewers/composite/languageClient.ts): findings appear as you type, hover shows a process's interface, and completion offers processes, ports, config keys and stores, all from the manifest of the environment picked above the editor. Run compiles the text in the browser (addresses in the local:module.Class form the service accepts; sidecar files compiled back in) and submits the document as a .pbg to /simulation/run in that environment.

get-simulations-status-batch is not used: it is a GET with a JSON body, which browsers cannot send. The list page re-fetches while any row is still running.

docs.title: How it is built and served
docs.text:
• npm run generate writes static files to webapp/.output/public. The image builds them in a Node stage of Dockerfile-api and copies them in.
  • compose_api/api/webapp.py mounts that directory at /ui when it exists (settings.webapp_dist_dir). A path without a file suffix gets the app shell (200.html), so deep links work. Without a build, the API runs as before.
  • The API calls are typed from the committed OpenAPI spec. npm run types (also run by make clients) regenerates webapp/app/api/schema.d.ts with openapi-typescript, and the calls go through openapi-fetch. CI fails if that file is stale. Never hand-edit it.
  • There is no ingress change: the existing / → api:8000 rule already covers /ui.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text:
The API accepts anonymous calls (Authentication), so the UI works without signing in. The UI offers an Auth0 login (@auth0/auth0-vue, after the platform frontend's plugin) only when the API publishes all three of these at GET /webapp/config:

Setting Meaning AUTH0_DOMAIN the tenant, shared with token verification AUTH0_AUDIENCE the API identifier the UI requests a token for AUTH0_SPA_CLIENT_ID an Auth0 Single Page Application whose allowed callback, logout and web origins include https://compose.cam.uchc.edu/ui/ (and http://localhost:4200/ui/ for development), and which may request that audience

Rules for the token:

  • Only API requests carry it: a request gets the token only when its destination is the API's own origin and path (app/utils/apiAuth.ts, after the platform's isPlatformApiRequest), never another host or a lookalike.
  • When the API rejects it (401), the UI drops it, carries on anonymously, and shows a banner. It does not retry.
  • When the session can no longer be renewed (the refresh token expired or was revoked), the UI signs the person out locally and says so, with a button to sign in again.
  • Downloads by a signed-in user are fetched with the token, because a plain link cannot carry the header.
  • After sign-in the UI asks GET /auth/me who the caller is, once. A token the API rejects shows up at once, and the account menu lists the roles the API sees.
  • "Create account" opens Auth0's sign-up page. Signing in returns to the page the person started from.
  • The account menu shows what the API says the caller may do (capabilities from GET /auth/me); with environments:admin it links "You can administer environments".

The token is kept in the browser's local storage, with rotating refresh tokens, as the platform frontend does (decision D1 in plan-webapp-login). Because script injection could read it, every /ui response carries these security headers:

  • A Content-Security-Policy that allows scripts only from this origin, plus the hashes of the build's inline scripts, which the API computes from the files it serves. Connections are allowed only to this origin and the Auth0 tenant. The page cannot be framed. Production enforces it (WEBAPP_CSP_ENFORCE=true); without that setting it only reports. Browsers post violations to POST /webapp/csp-report, which the API logs as CSP violation report.
  • X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.

A token changes nothing a caller can read, because every simulation is public. It changes what a caller may do only through the capabilities below.

The SPA applications are created by auth0-pulumi (UCHHPC/auth0-pulumi#5): p7uif3ex4LijqPwSOJsPBnhCdClnxSMM for production, whose callbacks also include the dev server's, and fEbf0F5Orb6FD4TySB8yWSZTj5hhBNJV for the local cluster. Their ids are set in kustomize/config/compose-api-rke/api.env and kustomize/overlays/compose-api-local/auth0.env.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text:
Environment versions are administered on the environment's own page (plan-webapp-admin, A2), not in a separate area. The controls appear only when GET /auth/me lists environments:admin, which a caller has when they hold the deployment's ENVIRONMENT_ADMIN_ROLE (production: the tenant's admin role). The UI only displays the capability: the API checks every request again and answers 403 to anyone else, so a hidden button is never the protection.

Action Offered for What it does New version a composed environment (registry_env, a mash-up) resolves its registry entries as of a date (today: now) and locks them, then builds the image and runs its compliance cases; an identical lock gives the existing version Register an image a prebuilt environment registers an image by digest (repository@sha256:…; tags are refused), pulls it and reads it back Make default a ready version that is not the default runs that name no version run in it; recorded runs and suite runs, which name their versions, do not change Retire a ready or failed version that is not the default it refuses new runs; recorded runs keep it, and its images are kept Re-read contents a ready version, or any prebuilt image runs its image again, in the background, to record what it installed and the classes it provides; a build does this by itself, so it is for a prebuilt image or a record that is missing or wrong. Runs and the default are unaffected

Every action is confirmed in a dialog that names the environment, the version and the effect (A3). Making a version the default shows its packages against the current default's (?against=), since a new version changes nothing until it is the default. After a new version is made, the page follows it every five seconds until it is ready or failed, and shows why it failed. Custom library lists are not offered: that path is retired (composition D8.5).

The same actions are compose-api environments create|default|retire|inspect on the command line.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
nvm use                   # Node 24: webapp/.nvmrc, linked from the repo root's .nvmrc (CI reads the same file)
make webapp-install       # npm ci
make run                  # the API on :8000
make webapp-dev           # the UI on http://localhost:4200/ui/, calling the API on :8000
COMPOSE_API_URL=https://compose.cam.uchc.edu make webapp-dev   # against production instead (CORS allows :4200)
make webapp-check         # lint, typecheck, API types current
make webapp-build         # static build; `make run` then serves it at http://localhost:8000/ui/

To sign in from the dev server against make run, set AUTH0_AUDIENCE and AUTH0_SPA_CLIENT_ID in .dev_env as .dev_env_TEMPLATE describes: the production SPA is the only one whose callbacks include http://localhost:4200/ui/.

npm audit reports advisories in build-time tooling (the Nitro dev server and its dependencies). None of it ships: the image serves only the generated static files.

docs.title: Toward one frontend with the platform
docs.text:
The platform frontend is server-rendered and deployed on GKE (biosim.biosimulations.org). This UI is static and served by the API on the on-premise RKE2 cluster (compose.cam.uchc.edu). Because they share a stack, components move between the two without rewriting. There are two ways to reconcile them:

  1. The platform frontend gains a compose backend. These pages become a section of the platform app with a configurable base URL for this API, and /ui here is retired. This needs CORS for the platform origin and the same Auth0 audience setup.
  2. Nuxt layers. These pages ship as a Nuxt layer that both apps extend: the platform app on GKE, and a thin shell here for the on-premise deployment.
